"Arcanum : Engrenages et Sortilèges" est le jeu que j'ai tant joué durant mon enfances, de mes 7 8 ans à aujourd'hui à mes 30 ans, j'y es tellement joué avec la version CD de l'époque (malheuresement CD casser au bout de nombreuse utilisation) Quand j'ai vu qu'il était sur Steam j'ai été tellement heureux et nostalgique que je l'ai prit directement ... dommage il est en anglais ... oh mince j'ai patché le jeu en FR en 5 minutes chrono, et hop comme mon enfance et adolescence ... comme quoi avec un minimum d'efforts Steam aurait pu le mettre en place pour nous les francophones...)

Ce jeu est très ambitieux pour un jeu de 2001, avec son jeu de rôles avec son ambiance particulière et d'une profondeur peu commune .

Le fait de pouvoir faire évoluer un personnage de base ou le crée et vivre dans un monde ou la magie ancestrale qui à du mal à survire et une pleine révolution industrielle, je trouve cela génial ... Ce thème qui est le coeur du jeu et l'histoire : MAGIE vs. TECHNOLOGIE.

Le fait de pouvoir voir pas moins de 76 lieux différent à découvrir en avançant sur la cartes ; Cette aventure non-linéaire m'a entrainer dans plein de lieu et de découverte passionnante . 

Tout cela pour dire que si vous aimé les RPG, foncer ... vous aller adoré ! car moi avec les heures passé pendant mon enfance et adolescence et là maintenant, je me suis régalé et je me régale encore ...

- un demi-ogre hérité d'une bonne bourse (é_è),
- une nain maitre en magie orphelin,
- une elfe du coté maléfique pactisé avec un démon

Saying Planescape: Torment has the greatest story ever told in an RPG is like saying water is wet. It's almost annoying to read at this point because it has been declared ad nauseam, but truly I can not go a week without thinking about the game narratively and thematically. The same thing for me applies to Arcanum here as well. It lead me to think about Role-Playing Games in regard to narrative itself. The recent gold-standard champion for so many being Baldur's Gate 3.

I don't think Baldur's Gate 3's throughline narrative is ... well, I don't think it's amazing. It's fine. I think for most people, it serves as a backdrop to experience the real rich storytelling that comes through with your party. The insane production values combined with all the differing stories of each party member is where most of the ballyhoo comes from. Now admittedly, I'm not 'as' nuts over the characters and their stories as some are and have yacked about how I actually think Dragon Age: Origins (the BG3 of its era) character stories are more compelling to me personally, but where BG3 really hit for me was its mix of gameplay where its foundation is basically an isometric immersive sim crossed with classic RPG mechanics as well. That was dope.

The actual narrative itself though? It's merely 'fine'. Thinking about this had me kind of evaluating what I value the most in the genre and it's certainly the big narrative and its themes and its world. Games like Arcanum or Planescape: Torment are loaded with a lot of parroting criticism over its mechanics/gameplay being awful, which I think is overblown. I don't think each games gameplay is amazing mind you, but I do think they're mostly 'fine'. It gets the job done. The plot/narrative and their themes and world though? Very few games contend to me. This applies entirely to Morrowind as well.

Most fantasy RPG games tend to be written/built around 'preservation'. You know the classic ♥♥♥♥ of old ass kingdoms needing a hero to restore them to their former glory; the sacred traditions preserved and protected all formed around you defeating an evil dark lord and such. A genre where history is in decline: The old world was greater, its people more unified and spiritually more cohesive. The hero is here to save what remains of this world before evil conquers and it disappears forever.

Arcanum is not that game. In fact, Arcanum is almost a near opposite of this often-imitated idea. In Arcanum, its world is not falling into ruin/collapse but accelerating drastically into 'modernity'. You have factories spread across its landscapes which were once happily dominated by forests or temples. Railroads connect cities/nations replacing what magic ever did. Industrial capital reshapes the political power at hand. Entire races become economically obsolete in this modern world. The core central theme is not that civilization is ending, but that civilization is transforming and evolving so rapidly that its people do not fully understand what is being lost in the process.

Essentially it's the general tension between progress and the spiritual erosion that basically defines nearly every aspect of the games narrative / world.

Coming into the game for the first time, any given player at first glance might see the game as a strange/unusual fusion of fantasy and steampunk (and it is as well): You have elves that exist alongside steam engines, dwarves live in their mountains or in cities but build firearms, magic users move about by streets lit with electricity etc etc. You soon understand the core idea in that magic and technology are fundamentally incompatible systems. Tech people become so rationally aligned with physical law that magical forces cease to function, while the spiritual and magically inclined folk disrupt machines simply by being even near them. Magic represents intuition, mysticism, spirituality and tradition; we have technology on the other end representing industrialization, rationalism, capitalism and mass production.

A lesser game would make it clear which side is better, Arcanum will not fully romanticize either end of the spectrum and it is so much better for it.

The magically inclined societies of this world are not some simple enlightened utopias. Elven culture is often depicted as aristocratic, stagnant and extremely hierarchical. As in the real world we live in now, tradition 'can' preserve wisdom, but without caution, can also preserve injustice as well. Meanwhile, industrial civilization can lead to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ extraordinary innovation, yet it simultaneously creates exploitation and dehumanization. Arcanum understands industrial progress as a morally double-edged sword: Technological innovation improves lives while also reducing people into economic functions. Who would have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thought lmao.

All of this sorta coalesces into the treatment of different races and labor. The games cities are filled with displaced workers and impoverished people, and nonhuman races marginalized and pushed to the side by modernization.

You get shredded by Half-Ogre bandits aboard the zeppelin and crash killing everybody on board. Everybody but you. How in the world did these machines exist? From there, you follow a trail and investigation into hidden histories, lost civilizations and manipulated truths (it's crazy this and Morrowind came out only a few months apart lol). The deeper you dig into it all, the more unstable official history becomes. All these ancient myths contradict all the archaeological evidence you uncover. Political narratives fall apart; collapse under the weight of scrutiny. Religious truths reveal themselves as falsehoods, incomplete or distorted. It reinforces that history is often not objective memory but constructed or even fabricated mythology.

All of this comes to a real head with the main narrative drive of the game: Nasrudin / Arronax / Kerghan. Kerghan is banished to the Void for defying the councils rule and before him, the same for Arronax as well. Nasrudin is then remembered and worshiped as the lands greatest hero. This narrative slowly unravels as you uncover that Arronax isn't as he seems, nor is Nasrudin and moreso that Kerghan is not your conventional fantasy villain bent on conquest or domination. Instead, he is almost a philosopher driven by profound despair about the nature of existence itself. Kerghan in many ways is the equal of sorts to Cain's previous games lead antagonist: The Master. Kerghan's view of the world comes about from witnessing the endless cycles of suffering throughout its history. A world where people repeatedly create war, exploitation, inequality and death. Progress for the sake of progress leading into suffering instead of eliminating it itself. From his perspective, existence is fundamentally cruel, and death becomes the only universal solution. His plan to extinguish life mirrors the same understood reasoning as what The Masters ideals were in Fallout. Naturally both are so fundamentally flawed, but both exist in a way that the player can sympathize with their problematic train of thought. Neither is cartoonishly evil.

Kerghan, alongside The Master and The Transcendent One, manages to be a wholly more compelling antagonist than 'most' role-playing game antagonists ever manage. He does not merely appose the player on the grounds of being a simple evil bad guy, he challenges the moral foundations underlying civilization itself. The final confrontation is less Good vs Evil or Evil vs Evil, instead its more akin to debating nihilism. (Or contributing toward it lol).

The legendary Troika Games was founded by three legendary developers upon three great principles: design, art, and code; they made three broken masterpieces. Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura is one of them. There was a reason why Troika went bankrupt: you can't rely just on great ideas alone; you also have to implement them well and manage your resources. Arcanum has a fantastic premise: a magical world going through an industrial revolution. And the setting is the only good thing about this game. All the rest is just painful.

I've tried this game a couple of times years earlier, and I can't do it anymore. My first two runs were gunslinger. It sounds cool, but the gameplay is awful, or more awful than usual. I'd suggest staying away from guns on your first playthrough. Some say that tech builds are the most fun way to play the game. I don't know. Arcanum is an exercise in tedium. The UI in general, and the inventory system specifically, is cumbersome. For tech you have to juggle inventory a lot between your companions, because you can't hold much, not by weight, but by volume. You can't stack your ingredients, and notes and quest items are huge. So, the less you have to interact with inventory management, the better. The camera is locked to your party for some reason. At first, it was just annoying, but when you travel to Tarant, which is a massive city, it becomes a real problem. Navigation is plain bad, and it will test your patience.

The third time I said to hell with guns, I would just whack enemies with my sword and be done with it. I imagined a human, maybe a doctor, who sees the changes in the world and would embrace technological progress, the new way of living. But technology is just tedium. Magic can do everything tech can, and even more. It’s easier and even more fun, for example, conjuring spirits of the dead. And the combat… oh god, the combat. The publisher Sierra, after Diablo’s success, insisted on real-time battles in the middle of production. So now we got two broken systems. Fantastic!

Character creation and progression are not as fun compared to Fallout with its perks. Upon creation you only have five points for everything. That’s not enough to make a distinct character. It’s only possible if you choose an extreme background paired with extreme races.

You’d think the writing would at least be great. Nope. It’s serviceable, but nothing special. They spent countless hours writing different flavors of dialogue for drunk or stupid characters, and different greetings for different races. But there is no depth to it, at least in the first third of the game. For persuasion you need to orient yourself in a dialogue tree, not just pick options with [persuasion] in them, which is great. So, the writing is fine, it’s okay, I just expected much more. Quests are meh. I guess all the interesting stuff is further into the story. But why should you torture yourself with this boring gameplay just to finally be hooked on good writing, pacing, and quest design far into the game?

The game is unfinished and poorly balanced. It has a gorgeous OST — beautiful, moody string quartet. It has great immersive manual. But it should have stayed in development at least a year longer: to make one good combat system, to finish the UI, and to smooth out pacing and balance issues. I wish there would be a remake, but it won’t happen.

My favorite game of all times and probably the only one that I replay every damn year (there are hundreds of hours I spent playing it throughout my life). Bought it on steam just to respect it by having in my library. 

Now, I admit there is a significant nostalgia factor, but still - this game is a cult classic ama lemme tell you why. 

It has a good, intricate story, exquisite dialogues (they are very rarely voiced but the quality of voice acting is top notch), interesting characters to meet and (arguably) fun character creation/development process. But the best things about it is the world/setting itself and the freedom of choice game grants you. As you may already know, it's steampunk game with the main motif of technology vs magic confrontation, but there there are still nothing quite like it to this day, it's a masterpiece execution. Also, the soundtrack is truly God-like. 

On the bad side, most people would say graphics are outdated (even I though I myself never thought that way), vanilla game is still full of unpleasant bugs, companions are not as charismatic as they are in, let's say, BG2. Also, game's combat is probably one of its most questionable areas. To me it's fun but for modern gamers it may look extremely clunky and counter-intuitive. 

To any RPG lovers I highly recommend at least to give this game a try. 
Trust me, it is cult classic for a good reason.

This is one of those games that has a ton of heart. But polish? Nope. The combat is extremely boring at best. 90% of the fights in Arcanum are against filler trash mobs that you can't skip, unlike Fallout. There is barely any encounter design in the entire game. I played a technologist gunslinger and they were hilariously weak compared to melee or magic characters. Luckily I followed guides so I knew how to craft the best items in the game, otherwise I might have quit out of frustration. 

The combat and balance are the game's biggest sins by far. The story is pretty good. The setting is amazing. A fantasy world going through an industrial revolution? Pure narrative gold. The main villain of the story is very intelligent and conniving, which I always like. I don't think he holds a candle to villains like The Master or Jon Irenicus, who feel a lot more sad and pitiable, but I appreciate that he has a philosophy that drives him to commit terrible acts. It's just good writing. 

With a couple more years in the oven I think this could have been one of the greatest games of all time. It's definitely worth picking up if you're willing to stomach bad combat for good story. I think it's a 6 or 7/10. I hope it gets a sequel one day.

You could probably pretty accurately guess if you'd enjoy this game or not before playing it. 

The real selling point is the world of Arcanum itself. The rise of technology in a previously magic-centric fantasy setting is interesting on its own, but its really clear the writers put a lot of thought into the many ways this might affect the people of Arcanum. Almost every conflict you encounter is a result of the struggle between these two forces. This is all backed up by very engaging dialogue and impressive attention to detail (things like how the newspapers change, being questioned about your ability to use magick before boarding the train).

The combat is probably better than you would expect if you've heard anything about this game before, but its definitely not a highlight.

Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura – игра особенная. А если вы пытались пройти ее на релизе, из раза в раз ловя софтлоки возле Гилберта Бейтса, который пропускал тебя дальше по сюжету только в качестве случайности… Тарант, музыка, полновесная вариативность отыгрыша с выбором не только между магами и техниками. Скажем, мое последнее прохождение было за очень харизматичного гнома, который не умел ни драться, ни собирать из хлама автоматонов, ни кастовать большую часть игры первый спелл некромантии. Он умел только пи… общаться. И торговать. И своей торговлей он одел своих шестерых спутников в лучшую броню, выдал им лучшее оружие и просто смотрел, как они убивают все живое. Так он и победил всех и вся, не убив своим руками вообще никого. И это даже не нечто особенное, обычный ран за гнома. 

Наверное, это одна из немногих игр, которую я никогда не удаляю с компа. Some games are good. Some games are unforgettable. Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura was unforgettable.

This was a hidden gem of isometric RPGs and discovering it during my childhood felt like finding a treasure. The world was unlike anything else, a gritty mix of industrial steamworks and high fantasy magic that somehow worked perfectly together. What blew me away most was the depth of customisation. Technology or magic? Charming diplomat or ruthless assassin? Every stat point, every skill choice mattered. And the story… I couldn’t wait to uncover more.

The choices genuinely puzzled me, in the best way. Decisions shaped your character’s identity and how the world reacted to you. I felt the consequences of morality. And the spell animations; I still remember them. There was something mesmerising about casting magic in that world, but what truly stuck with me was being able to summon the ghosts of the dead and speak with them to resolve quests.

Arcanum was and still is bold and incredibly unique. A true hidden gem that I will always cherish.

Would I reccomend Arcanum? Ehhhh, it's complicated. I'm leaning towards Yes, but only if you meet a few criteria:

- You enjoy Fallout 1 & 2 and wish to have a similar itch scratched (as the game was made with Tim Cain as project lead, in a very similar engine.)

- Combat is not very important to you and you're willing to slog through it.

- You don't mind long paragraphs of text.

If you meet those criteria, you will absolutely love Arcanum. It's a rich world full of lore and intrigue and a genuinely fascinating and memorable story. The amount of content it has to offer is absurd, rivalling modern RPGs, and is incredibly well written. The side content is often just as good as the main story, and the amount of possibilites you have for different builds is quite frankly baffling in it's scope.

This is a masterpiece that's hiding behind a clunky engine and pacing issues, but anyone who appreciates the qualities I mentioned in a game will find a lot to love.

Arcanum is a brilliant RPG, and one that I would argue is in contender for the best in it's genre. What it lacks in some mechanics and controls features (which is mostly a testament to its age) it makes up for with the most compelling open world setting I think I've played in a game.

The controls and general gameplay mechanics feel weird at first, but are quite intuitive once you've actually learnt them. Its biggest flaw is that most things are explained in the manual, meaning you sort of learn the controls as you go along, discovering features like how to use the quick bar or deploy a mechanical spider on the fly. Once you're past that difficulty spike, the mechanics of the game are quite fleshed out. The schematic system is extensive, the items and craftables feel near limitless. Overall its a very mechanically dense game.

The worlds story feels wasted on the game its found itself in, and im honestly amazed its never been adapted into a show or sequels after it released. Its concept is such unique ground to set a DND world in that most interactions and story beats are so unpredictable compared to your average RPG. The characters are all very fleshed out, the world and its environments are incredibly complex, and overall the way that NPCs and books talk about the world builds such a vivid picture compared to others in the genre.

The combat leaves much to be desired. Where i think they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up was in making the spells and high-end weapons too easy to aquire and too powerful. This means that many monsters lategame will kill a party member in 2-3 hits before you can even prevent it. I would much rather feel less overpowered and have less spiky combats than the state its in now, especially given the setting. The combat options intensify this, the turn based combat is pretty good but the initiative still feels random and causes you to suffer the same issues but slower. The real time on the other hand is a complete gamble of chaos mostly determined by how you're characters do damage. For example, playing as a summoner I could easily agro enemies, and have my monsters kill them before they even change attacker. This meant my strategy was to pull enemies, then run until they die. This is stopped when the enemy has a bow, in which I die to 10 arrows before I can even enter turn based mode.

The appeal of this game is mostly in the story and the world. And as someone who didn't play 90s RPGs I can safely say the graphics do not pull you away from that feeling. Its still just as interesting to explore as the day it released, and I can honestly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of narrative games. You can hate the combat, the gameplay, the leveling system and most mechanics with it and still come out of this game feeling like you enjoyed it more than you didn't just off the strength of the world. The world really is just that good and its why someone like me is even recommended it in the first place.
